newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: INTERVIEW - Gloomy '97 in store for Smurfit.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Gloomy '97 in store for Smurfit.

text.p: Irish paper and packaging manufacturer Jefferson Smurfit Group Plc on Tuesday held out a fragile hope that prices for the troubled industry may have bottomed out but the general outlook for 1997 remains gloomy.
Smurfit reported a drop of 52 percent in 1996 pre-tax profit to 204 million Irish pounds ($316.2 million) on turnover of 2,594 million Irish pounds down from 3,033 million in 1995.
"It is true that, all over, times are tough and the U.S. is probably the toughest market at this time," finance director Ray Curran told Reuters in an interview.

Curran said the group had been pretty consistent in expressing the view that a turn in prices would come sometime in 1997 but he did not disagree with analysts' forecasts that the group would see a further decline in profits in 1997.

"Pricing in 1997 is on average poorer than in 1996 and so the logic of that is that it would flow through to the bottom line," Curran said. "We will still be strongly profitable as a company but at what level we wouldn't be allowed to call and would not want to call."
He said price falls had been particularly sharp in the U.S. but paradoxically this was against a background where the industry had been performing strongly in operations terms.

"Volumes have been significantly up on 1996, meaning demand is strong, and the economy is in good shape but if anything it would be true that things have got weaker in pricing terms in the U.S. despite a strong demand pattern," Curran said.

The average price for linerboard, which accounts for more than 60 percent of Smurfit's volumes, fell to $375 a tonne in 1996 from just over $500 a tonne in 1995 and industry analysts say market conditions remain difficult following a failure to push through a $30 price increase in linerboard late last year.
"The problem is oversupply which has led to poor pricing, so we are busy but not profitable," Curran said.
Smurfit said in its results statement that between 1994 and 1997 the U.S. industry will show an annualised capacity growth rate of 4.5 percent.

"I think it is true to say that the world has seen the greatest party ever at the stock market level but the paper and packaging industry has not been invited, principally because of the undisciplined use of capital," Curran said.

He said the market will not accept for long an industry which has not earned its cost of capital in seven of the last 10 years. "1997 is very difficult from the standpoint of our shareholders we ourselves won't cover the cost of capital in 1997."

He said despite the troubled industry Smurfit's balance sheet remained very strong and debt was reduced by about 100 million Irish pounds in 1996 and year-end gearing levels were as low as 34 percent.
Curran said Smurfit continued to seek acquisitions particularly in Europe, Latin America and Asia.

"We have always used the cycle to our advantage and sought to acquire when the industry was in poor shape and we continue to look at opportunities wherever opportunities appear but it is unlikely that we will do anything major in 1997 other than bolt-on acquisitions." ($ = 0.645 Irish Pounds)
